--- title: "Surveillance and outbreak response" subtitle: "Where to sample, and what to do when something is already spreading" description: "Biodiversity-informed wildlife disease surveillance, and earlier outbreak response work on COVID-19 and mpox." categories: [Surveillance, One Health, Outbreak Response] toc: true execute: echo: false warning: false message: false --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} Placeholder page. Framing text is a draft. This page absorbs the former COVID-19 and mpox theme pages, which is why those sections are written in the past tense. Explainer notes for the papers are in `data/paper_notes/`. ::: Surveillance is a resource allocation problem before it is a laboratory one. Sampling wildlife is expensive, so the question is where a sample changes what we know. Outbreak response is the same question under time pressure. ## Wildlife disease surveillance **A protocol for biodiversity-informed wildlife disease surveillance.** *PLOS Ecosystems*, 2026. Host species distribution models set a biodiversity dose, uncertainty identifies where discovery sampling would help most, and balanced-acceptance sampling turns the result into field sites. Case studies on *Hantaviridae* and *Arenaviridae* in India and South Korea. Ongoing work extends this to outbreak settings, where the sampling frame has to be revised as an event unfolds. ## Directing rodent sampling *An AI-directed One Health risk prediction framework for active learning in rodent-borne zoonoses* is a Vetenskapsrådet South Korea–Sweden research collaboration grant, running from October 2026 to December 2027. I lead it from Uppsala University, with Chungnam National University as the Korean partner. The project combines three components. Landscape embeddings from Earth-observation imagery describe habitat, Bayesian spatial models downscale host hazard to human incidence, and an active-learning step directs rodent sampling to sites where a new sample would most reduce uncertainty and that a field team can reach. It builds on the South Korea case study in the protocol above. ## mpox Work from the 2022 outbreak and from the endemic range that preceded it. **Increased outbreaks of mpox highlight gaps in actual disease burden.** *International Journal of Infectious Diseases*, 2022. Two hypotheses for the global outbreak: growing synanthropic rodent populations in West and Central Africa, and an immunologically naive population 45 years after smallpox vaccination ended. **Community transmission of mpox in the United Kingdom.** *Eurosurveillance*, 2022. The first UK cases without travel history, described during the investigation, from work in the UK Health Security Agency outbreak surveillance team. The reservoir of mpox virus is still unidentified. Virus has been isolated from wild animals twice, and antibodies have been found in several further species. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

That work is finished. The papers are listed on the [publications page](/publications.html). ![Time to detection of different SARS-CoV-2 variants in the United Kingdom.](/images/covid_variant_spread.png) ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} To add: a short account of the UKHSA surveillance work. ::: ## Papers ::: {.pub-entry .pub-entry-plain #pub-10_1371_journal_pesy_0000023} ::: {.pub-body} **A protocol for biodiversity-informed wildlife disease surveillance** Catchen MD, Banville F, Boutin AC, Brookson CB, Carlson CJ, Dansereau G, …, **Simons D**, et al. [Preprint, 2025](https://doi.org/10.32942/x21d36) · [*PLOS Ecosystems*, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pesy.0000023) · [PDF](https://journals.plos.org/ecosystems/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pesy.0000023&type=printable)
Summary ::: {.pub-more-body} ![Sampling priority from host distribution models, and the choice of what to sample where.](/policy/images/bon_framework.png){.pub-fig fig-alt="Two-panel conceptual framework. On the left, sampling priority derived from host species distribution models and pathogen prevalence. On the right, the choice between prevalence and occurrence sampling given biodiversity dose and uncertainty."} Wildlife disease surveillance is expensive, and for most of the globe there is no actionable information on pathogen prevalence in host populations. Where data exist they have largely been collected opportunistically, without reference to the known distributions of hosts of zoonotic pathogens. This protocol adapts the Biodiversity Observation Network concept from biodiversity monitoring to biosurveillance. Local host composition is summarised as a biodiversity dose, a weighted average of habitat suitability scores from species distribution models capturing both likely presence and relative importance in transmission. Uncertainty extracted from the same models identifies where host occurrence sampling would most improve baseline predictions. An adaptive priority score balances discovery sampling in high-uncertainty regions against prevalence sampling where dose is high, and balanced-acceptance sampling then generates spatially balanced sites rather than clustering within autocorrelated priority areas. Two case studies on *Hantaviridae* and *Arenaviridae* in rodents demonstrate the range, India as a data-poor context calling for discovery sampling and South Korea as a data-rich one supporting spatially explicit prevalence estimates. The framework keeps the distinction between hazard and realised risk explicit throughout. :::
